traveler: Rabia al-Adawiyya (Rābi'a bint Ismā'īl al-'Adawiyya al-Qaysiyya)
title: Basra to Mecca and Back to Basra: the Torch, the Water, and the Love Without Cause
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Basra: The Fourth Daughter, Born to Want

stops.name: Basra, her father's house, the night of no oil
stops.campa: In a poor house of Basra a fourth daughter is born, and there is not one drop of oil in the house to anoint her navel, no lamp, no rag to swaddle her in. Her father, sworn by covenant never to beg of any mortal, will not even ask the neighbor for oil; his wife weeps. He sleeps and dreams the Prophet, who tells him the girl is a queen among women, intercessor for seventy thousand of his people, and sends him to the governor of Basra for four hundred lawful dinars. He wakes weeping, and writes as he was bidden.
stops.quote: The girl child who has just come to earth is a queen among women, who shall be the intercessor for seventy thousand of my community.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. A. J. Arberry, Muslim Saints and Mystics
suggested_refs: The maqam and mosque tradition of Rabia al-Adawiyya at Basra, held to mark her father's house
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry, Muslim Saints and Mystics, 1966)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic and Her Fellow-Saints in Islam (1928)

stops.name: Basra, the famine, and the six dirhams
stops.campa: Rabia is still young when her mother and father die and a famine falls on Basra; her three sisters are scattered to the winds of want. Venturing into the streets for bread, she is seen by a wicked man who seizes the orphaned girl and sells her in the market for six dirhams, a price the tradition never lets her or her hearers forget. Her purchaser sets her to hard labor by day. Nothing yet marks her as a queen among women except the covenant her father swore, which she now unknowingly inherits: to ask nothing of any creature.
suggested_refs: The six dirhams, the sum fixed in every later telling of her enslavement
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)

stops.name: Basra, the road, the fall, and the broken hand
stops.campa: Passing along a Basra road on some errand of her master's, Rabia sees a strange man approach and flees him. She falls headlong; her hand is dislocated in the fall. Bowing her face to the ground where she lies, a slave, an orphan, a stranger with a broken hand, she does not ask to be spared the fall's pain, only whether God is pleased with her or not. A voice answers her out of the ground itself, promising a station envied by the cherubim of heaven. She rises and returns to her master's house unhealed but unafraid.
stops.quote: Lord God, I am a stranger, orphaned of mother and father, a helpless prisoner fallen into captivity, my hand broken. Yet for all this I do not grieve; all I need is Thy good pleasure, to know whether Thou art well-pleased or no.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The broken hand, the first of her recorded prayers
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the master's window, the lantern without a chain
stops.campa: By day Rabia fasts and serves; by night she stands in prayer until dawn, telling God that if the choice were hers she would never rest an hour from His service, only He has set her under the hand of a creature. One night her master wakes, looks through the window, and sees her bowing in prayer beneath a lantern hung with no chain, its light filling the whole house. Afraid, he sits pondering until morning, then calls her, is gentle with her, and sets her free. She asks only his leave to go, and receives it.
stops.quote: O God, Thou knowest that the desire of my heart is in conformity with Thy command, and that the light of my eye is in serving Thy court. If the affair lay with me, I would not rest one hour from serving Thee, but Thou Thyself hast set me under the hand of a creature.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The lantern suspended without a chain above her head, the sign given to her master
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Rkia E. Cornell (tr.), Early Sufi Women: Sulami's Dhikr an-Niswa (1999)

segments.name: The Desert and the Vow Not to Ask

stops.name: Beyond Basra, the desert, the leaving of the house
stops.campa: Freed, Rabia does not seek a husband, a trade, or a patron among the pious of Basra who would gladly have taken in so marked a girl. She walks out past the last walls and gardens into the waste places, carrying nothing that binds her to a roof. The desert that swallows caravans and unmakes travelers receives her instead as a threshold. She has already, in her master's house, learned to want only one thing; the desert simply removes every other thing that could be wanted, leaving her the room in which to want it without division.
suggested_refs: The desert margin south and west of Basra, threshold of her withdrawal
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)

stops.name: A hermitage in the wilderness, the covenant of forty years
stops.campa: From the desert Rabia comes to a hermitage and settles to serve God there, alone, for what will become the rest of her long life. Here she binds herself by a vow the tradition will quote for forty years running: never to ask anything of any but Him. No neighbor's oil, no borrowed onion, no patron's purse will move her from this line, however plain her hunger or bare her house. The hermitage has no address the geographers keep, only the fact of it: a woman, a mat, a jar, and a covenant harder than the walls around her.
stops.quote: Forty years now I have had a covenant with Almighty God not to ask for aught of any but He.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Her reed mat, broken pitcher, and brick pillow, the whole furniture of the vow
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

segments.name: The Road to the House of God

stops.name: Basra, setting her face toward the desert road
stops.campa: In time Rabia determines to perform the pilgrimage, the duty owed once in a life to the House at Mecca. She binds her small bundle onto an ass and sets out from Basra along the desert road the pilgrim caravans keep, the same sands Basra's governors have dug wells along since the city's founding. She travels as she has lived, refusing company that would carry her burden for her, trusting the road to the same Providence that fed her onions and freed her from a lantern's witness. The house of God lies many hundred miles across the waste ahead.
suggested_refs: The Basra-Mecca pilgrim road, dug with wells since Abu Musa al-Ash'ari's governorship
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Muslim Heritage, 'Darb Zubayda: the overland Hajj route'

stops.name: Wadi al-Batin, the ass dies in the heart of the desert
stops.campa: At Wadi al-Batin, where the Basra road cuts into the emptiest of the desert crossing, Rabia's ass falls dead beneath its load. The men of the party offer to carry her bundle for her; she refuses them outright, having not set out trusting in men. Left alone in the waste, she lifts her face and asks whether kings treat a stranger and powerless woman so, invited to His house only to be abandoned in the road's middle with a dead beast for company. She does not curse the desert; she simply asks the House to answer for it.
stops.quote: O God, do kings so treat a woman who is a stranger and powerless? Thou hast invited me unto Thy house, then in the midst of the way Thou hast suffered my ass to die, leaving me alone in the desert.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Wadi al-Batin, the driest and hardest stage of the old Basra-Mecca road
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Muslim Heritage, 'Darb Zubayda: the overland Hajj route'

stops.name: The Ad-Dahna sands, the ass revived, the mountain and Moses
stops.campa: Her prayer scarcely finished, the dead ass stirs and rises; she loads her bundle again and goes on into the red dunes of the Dahna, the hardest belt of the whole crossing. Days later, spent, she halts and cries that her heart is weary, that she is only clay walking toward a house of stone, and that she needs Him here, now, not at the end of so much sand. God answers unmediated in her heart: she fares in the life-blood of eighteen thousand worlds; let her recall how Moses begged the vision and a mountain shattered for less.
stops.quote: Rabia, thou art faring in the life-blood of eighteen thousand worlds. Hast thou not seen how Moses prayed for the vision of Me? And I cast a few motes of revelation upon the mountain, and the mountain shivered into forty pieces. Be content here with My name!
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The Ad-Dahna sand belt, the hardest stage of the Basra-Mecca road
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Saudipedia, 'Historical Hajj Routes'

stops.name: Outskirts of Mecca, Ibrahim ibn Adham and the wandering Kaaba
stops.campa: Ibrahim ibn Adham, prince turned beggar, has spent fourteen years crossing this same desert on foot, praying two prostrations at every step, to reach the House. He arrives at last to find the Kaaba gone from its place, and a voice tells him it has moved to go and meet a woman who approaches. He runs and finds Rabia arriving, and the House already back on its foundation behind her. Fourteen years of prostrations, and a woman he has never met has drawn the House itself out to the road to greet her before he could finish his approach.
stops.quote: You have spent fourteen years in crossing the desert in ritual prayer; I have crossed it in personal supplication.
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (recorded in later redactions of Attar and Jami's Nafahat al-Uns)
suggested_refs: The meeting of Rabia and Ibrahim ibn Adham on the Mecca road, a set scene in later Persian miniature painting
sources: Jami, Nafahat al-Uns (15th c. redaction of the earlier hagiographic cycle)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba, 'the Lord of the house whom I need'
stops.campa: Rabia comes to the Kaaba at last, the black-draped House that has, the tradition says, come out on the road to meet her before she has even finished the last stage. She will not be satisfied with a building, however holy, however far she has walked to it. She circles it and speaks the sentence that becomes her name in every later telling of this scene: it is the Lord of the House she needs, not the House; stone has no power over her; only the promise that whoever approaches by a span will be met by a cubit answers her.
stops.quote: It is the Lord of the house whom I need, what have I to do with the house? I need to meet with Him Who said, 'Who approaches Me by a span's length, I will approach him by the length of a cubit.'
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (recorded in later redactions of Attar and Jami's Nafahat al-Uns)
suggested_refs: The Kaaba at Mecca, the House Rabia refuses to mistake for its Lord
sources: Jami, Nafahat al-Uns (15th c.)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)

stops.name: Basra, the return from the pilgrimage
stops.campa: The pilgrimage made, the vow discharged, Rabia turns back across the same desert road toward Basra and the hermitage she left. She brings back no relic, no souvenir of the House, only the sentence she spoke at it, which will outlast every stone of Mecca in the mouths of those who tell her story. She resumes the narrow life of fasting and night-prayer exactly where she set it down, as though the whole outward journey had been folded invisibly into the stillness she never really left. Basra receives her back as the same poor woman who departed, and greater.
suggested_refs: The Basra hermitage, resumed unchanged after the one great outward journey of her life
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)
Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the thief and the chaddur
stops.campa: Rabia falls asleep at prayer in her hermitage, so deeply that a reed breaks loose from her mat and cuts her eye without waking her. A thief slips in and seizes her chaddur, her only outer garment, and turns to leave; the way out is barred to him. He drops the cloth and finds the door open, picks it up again and finds it shut, seven times over, until a voice from the corner of the room tells him to stop troubling himself: the Devil himself dares not go near her, so how should a thief manage what the Devil cannot.
stops.quote: It is so many years now that she has committed herself to Us. The Devil himself has not the boldness to slink round her. How should a thief have the boldness to slink round her chaddur?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Rabia's chaddur, guarded by an unseen watch, in the popular telling of the hermitage tales
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, two hungry saints and twenty loaves
stops.campa: Two notables of the faith visit Rabia hungry, hoping her food at least will be lawfully come by. A napkin appears with two loaves; before they can eat, a beggar comes to the door and Rabia gives the loaves away, silently trusting the promise of tenfold return. A maidservant arrives soon after with eighteen warm loaves from her mistress; Rabia, counting, says this cannot be what was meant for her, and sends them back. Two more are found and added, making twenty; only then does she accept them and set the bread, doubled by her own arithmetic of trust, before her guests.
stops.quote: I said to myself, How can I offer two loaves to two such notables? So when the beggar came to the door I gave them to him and said to Almighty God, 'O God, Thou hast said that Thou repayest tenfold... Now I have given two loaves to please Thee, so that Thou mayest give twenty in return for them.'
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The twenty loaves, a favorite proof-text for Rabia's arithmetic of trust in the later tellings
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the onion stew and the bird
stops.campa: Rabia's servant girl, cooking an onion stew after days without proper food, finds she lacks onions and offers to ask the neighbors. Rabia will not hear of it: forty years now she has kept her covenant not to ask of any but God, and the onions can go unasked for. At once a bird drops out of the sky with peeled onions already in its beak and lets them fall into the pan. Even this Rabia will not trust outright, wondering aloud whether it is not some trick; she leaves the onion pulp untouched and eats plain bread instead, unaltered by the wonder.
stops.quote: Forty years now I have had a covenant with Almighty God not to ask for aught of any but He. Nevermind the onions.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The bird with peeled onions in its beak, one of the most quoted of her small wonders
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: The wild places beyond Basra, the deer and Hasan's question
stops.campa: Walking in the waste beyond the town, Rabia is ringed about by deer, mountain goats, ibexes and wild asses that come near her unafraid. Hasan of Basra, the great preacher, comes upon the scene and moves toward her; at his approach every animal bolts, leaving Rabia alone and Hasan dismayed. He asks why the creatures flee him and stay tame for her. She asks what he has eaten that day; a little onion pulp, he says. Then he eats their fat, she answers, so why should they not flee from him; her fast alone has kept her outside the food chain of fear.
stops.quote: You eat their fat. Why then should they not flee from you?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The deer and wild asses gathered fearlessly around Rabia, a recurring image in later Sufi painting
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the streets, the torch and the pail of water
stops.campa: Rabia is seen running through the streets of Basra with a lit torch in one hand and a pail of water in the other. Asked what she means by it, she answers that she means to set fire to Paradise and quench the flames of Hell with the water she carries, so that the two veils fall away and no one worships God any longer for fear of the one or hope of the other, but for Himself alone. The saying passes from mouth to mouth long after the torch has gone out, becoming the single sentence Basra will not let her live down or live without.
stops.quote: I want to burn Paradise with this fire and put out the flames of Hell with this water, so that these two veils disappear and nobody worships God out of fear of Hell or hope of Paradise, but seeks Him for Himself alone.
stops.quote_source: Sufi oral tradition, widely transmitted in varying wordings; no early primary attestation (see Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic, 1928)
suggested_refs: The torch and the pail of water, the single image by which Rabia is known outside the Sufi canon
sources: Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic and Her Fellow-Saints in Islam (1928)
Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (the doctrine of disinterested love this scene enacts)

stops.name: Basra, the Tigris bank, the blanket and the color that did not matter
stops.campa: Rabia gives a man four silver dirhams and asks him to buy her a blanket, for she goes without one. He returns before buying it to ask what color she prefers. The question itself offends her: how has color entered into this business at all, she demands, and takes the money back. Rather than let a shred of preference or vanity attach itself to so plain a need, she walks to the Tigris bank and flings the four dirhams into the river, choosing to go on cold and unblanketed rather than let the color of a covering become a want of its own.
stops.quote: How did 'colour' come into the business? Give me back the money.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The Tigris riverbank at Basra, where the four dirhams were thrown rather than kept
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, her doorway, 'come in and see the Maker'
stops.campa: On a spring morning Rabia's servant calls her out to see what the Maker has wrought: the gardens in flower, the light on the water, the whole visible splendor of the season. Rabia will not come out. She tells the girl to come in instead, and see the Maker, since the contemplation of Him so occupies her that she has no wish left over to look at what He has merely made. The line becomes a small doctrine in itself among those who hear it: that the works of God, however lovely, are a distraction from God once the heart has truly found Him.
stops.quote: Do you rather come in and see the Maker. The contemplation of the Maker preoccupies me, so that I do not care to look upon what He has made.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The spring gardens of Basra, refused in favor of the Maker behind them
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the meat torn by hand, for fear of the knife
stops.campa: Visitors find Rabia tearing a morsel of meat apart with her teeth rather than cutting it, and ask why she keeps no knife in her house. She answers that she has never kept one there, for fear of being cut off. The pun sits at the center of the household economy she has built for herself: no blade, no color of blanket, no borrowed onion, nothing that could sever her attention from the one relation that matters or introduce a second want beside the first. Her poverty is not accidental scarcity; it is a house deliberately emptied of anything sharp enough to interrupt her.
stops.quote: I have never kept a knife in my house for fear of being cut off.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The absent knife, the household detail most quoted for her deliberate self-emptying
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, her door, the bandage of complaint
stops.campa: A man comes to Rabia with a bandage tied round an aching head. She asks his age; thirty, he says. She asks whether he has spent the greater part of those thirty years in pain; no, he admits. Then, she says, for thirty years of good health he never once tied on himself the bandage of thankfulness, yet for one night's headache he ties the bandage of complaint without hesitation. The rebuke is gentle and total at once, weighing a single night's ache against three decades of unremarked mercy, and finding the ledger of human gratitude wanting on the larger, not the smaller, side.
stops.quote: For thirty years you have enjoyed good health, and you never tied about you the bandage of thankfulness. Now because of this one night that you have a headache you tie the bandage of complaint!
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The bandage of complaint, a proverb still repeated in Sufi teaching circles
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, a gathering, the debate on women and prophethood
stops.campa: A party of men comes to test Rabia, hoping to catch her in an unguarded word. All the virtues, they tell her, have been scattered on the heads of men; the crown of prophethood and the belt of nobility belong to men alone; no woman has ever been a prophet. She grants it freely, and answers that no woman, either, has ever risen up crying I am your Lord, the Most High, or made herself a hermaphrodite of vanity and self-worship as certain men have done; those particular sins, at least, remain the unchallenged specialty of the sex that claims every virtue for itself.
stops.quote: Egoism and self-worship and 'I am your Lord, the Most High' have never sprung from a woman's breast. No woman has ever been a hermaphrodite. All these things have been the specialty of men.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Attar's own prefatory defense of including a woman among the saints, framing this whole chapter
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

segments.name: Hasan of Basra: the Brother Who Could Not Fly

stops.name: Basra, Hasan's window, the tears that fell on her dress
stops.campa: Rabia passes beneath Hasan of Basra's window and feels drops falling on her dress; she takes them at first for rain, then looks up and sees the great preacher weeping at his sill. She tells him plainly that weeping of this kind is a sign of spiritual weakness, not strength, and that he should guard his tears until they gather into a sea deep enough that, searching his own heart within it, he finds nothing there except what is kept by an Omnipotent King. Hasan is distressed by the correction but says nothing, unable to answer a rebuke he cannot refute.
stops.quote: Master, this weeping is a sign of spiritual languor. Guard your tears, so that there may surge within you such a sea that, seeking the heart therein, you shall not find it save in the keeping of a King Omnipotent.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Hasan al-Basri's window, the recurring stage for his exchanges with Rabia in the tradition
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: A lake near Basra, the floating rug and the flight above it
stops.campa: Hasan meets Rabia by a lake and, to show his spiritual attainment, throws his prayer rug onto the surface of the water and calls her to pray two prostrations there with him. Rabia tells him that if he must display his spiritual goods in this worldly market, let it be something his fellow men cannot also do; then she flings her own rug into the air and rises to sit on it, calling him up where the people can see them better. Hasan, who has not reached that station, is silenced; she consoles him afterward that fish float and flies rise, and the real business lies past both tricks.
stops.quote: Hasan, what you did fishes also do, and what I did flies also do. The real business is outside both these tricks. One must apply one's self to the real business.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The floating prayer-rug and the rug that rose into the air, a paired image in Persian manuscript illustration
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, a night without a lantern, her shining finger
stops.campa: Hasan comes one night with two or three friends to visit Rabia, and finds she has no lantern lit in her hermitage; their hearts yearn for a little light to sit by. Rabia blows upon her own hunger, and from that breath her finger begins to shine like a lamp until dawn, giving the visitors light enough to sit in and talk by. The tradition defends the wonder by the same logic it uses for Moses' luminous hand: whoever walks closely enough in a prophet's footsteps may carry a grain of prophethood, however small, in an otherwise ordinary, famished body.
suggested_refs: Her shining finger, defended in the text by comparison to the luminous hand of Moses
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the wax, the needle, and the hair
stops.campa: Rabia sends Hasan three small objects with no letter of explanation: a piece of wax, a needle, and a hair. The message is meant to be read, not told: be like the wax, which lights the world by consuming itself; be like the needle, always at plain, naked work; and when both of these have been achieved, a thousand years will pass for you as lightly as a single hair. It is teaching reduced to its barest materials, the whole discipline of self-consuming service handed across Basra in a folded scrap of cloth rather than a sermon.
stops.quote: Be like wax. Illumine the world, and yourself burn. Be like a needle, always be working naked. When you have done these two things, a thousand years will be for you as a hair.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The wax, needle, and hair, quoted as a compressed rule of life in later Sufi manuals
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the proposal, 'being has disappeared'
stops.campa: Hasan asks Rabia at last whether she desires that they marry. She answers that the tie of marriage binds those who still possess a separate being to bind; in her, being has vanished, she exists only through Him and belongs wholly to Him, and lives in the shadow of His control alone. If Hasan wants her hand, she tells him, he must ask it of God, not of her. Pressed further for the secret of this state, she answers that she lost every 'found' thing in Him, and that where Hasan knows the how of knowing God, she knows only the howless.
stops.quote: The tie of marriage applies to those who have being. Here being has disappeared, for I have become naughted to self and exist only through Him. I belong wholly to Him. I live in the shadow of His control. You must ask my hand of Him, not of me.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The refused proposal of Hasan al-Basri, the most quoted of her marriage refusals
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

segments.name: The Emir's Letter and the Household of Women

stops.name: Basra, the Emir's letter of proposal
stops.campa: Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Hashimi, the Abbasid governor of Basra, sends to Rabia offering marriage, a great dowry, and an income that would end her poverty at a stroke. She answers him in a letter rather than in person, refusing not the man's rank but the whole shape of the offer: it would bring her no happiness, she writes, to have him owned by her or herself occupied by him, kept even for a glance from the one relation she has spent a lifetime narrowing her house to hold. The governor's wealth is declined as firmly as the poorest suitor's onions once were.
stops.quote: It brings me no happiness that you should become my slave, and that I should be owned by you, and that you should keep me occupied, away from Allah, even for a glance.
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (Ibn Khallikan; Jami, Nafahat al-Uns; popularized in Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic, 1928)
suggested_refs: The letter to the Emir of Basra, her most politically pointed refusal of marriage
sources: Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic (1928)
Jami, Nafahat al-Uns (15th c.)

stops.name: Basra, the household of women, Maryam and 'Abda
stops.campa: Around Rabia's hermitage a small household of women gathers who will not be sent home like the suitors. Maryam of Basra stands the whole night in ecstatic worship beside her, given to repeating God's own tenderness toward His servants until dawn finds her still standing. 'Abda bint Abi Shawwal binds herself to Rabia's service as her devoted attendant, present at the prayer vigils and, later, at the deathbed itself. Where the men of Basra bring proposals and purses, these women bring only their company, and it is this company, not any suitor's offer, that Rabia keeps.
suggested_refs: Maryam of Basra and 'Abda bint Abi Shawwal, recorded among the earliest named Sufi women
sources: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Dhikr an-Niswa al-Muta'abbidat as-Sufiyyat, tr. Rkia E. Cornell as Early Sufi Women (1999)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the illness that followed a vision of Paradise
stops.campa: Rabia falls gravely sick, and those around her ask the cause. She answers that she gazed upon Paradise, and her Lord disciplined her for the gazing, as though the reward itself were a distraction requiring correction. The illness settles over the hermitage that had until now been the scene mostly of small wonders and sharp sayings; now it becomes the site of a long dying, visited over the years by the same generation of Basra's ascetics who have argued with her, tested her, and loved her, come now to sit at the pillow of the woman who refused them all.
stops.quote: I gazed upon Paradise, and my Lord disciplined me.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: Rabia's sickbed, the setting for nearly all of the tradition's remaining anecdotes of her
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, her door, the notable's purse of gold
stops.campa: Hasan comes to visit the sick Rabia and finds at her hermitage door one of Basra's notables, weeping, holding out a purse of gold for her care and afraid she will refuse it. He asks Hasan to intercede for him. Rabia, told of the gift, answers that God provides for those who insult Him, so surely He provides for those who love Him; she does not know whether any man's wealth is lawfully come by, and cannot take what she cannot vouch for. She recalls mending a torn shirt once by lamplight and tearing the stitches out again rather than let the memory of that borrowed light trouble her heart.
stops.quote: He provides for those who insult Him, and shall He not provide for those who love Him? Ever since I knew Him, I have turned my back upon His creatures. I know not whether any man's property is lawful or not; how then can I take it?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The refused purse of gold, brought weeping to her sickbed door
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Sofyan al-Thawri and twelve years of dates
stops.campa: Abd al-Wahed-e Amer comes with Sofyan al-Thawri to visit the sick Rabia, too awed to speak first. Sofyan tells her to pray for ease from her pain; she asks whether it was not God who willed her to suffer it, and if so how Sofyan can bid her ask the contrary of His own will. Pressed for what she does desire, she confesses that for twelve years she has wanted fresh dates, cheap and common as they are in Basra, and has never once eaten one, since a servant of God has no business desiring anything her Lord has not Himself already given.
stops.quote: By the glory of God, for twelve years now I have been desiring fresh dates. You know that in Basra dates are of no consequence. Yet till now I have not eaten any; for I am His servant, and what business has a servant to desire?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The twelve years of undesired dates, her sharpest statement of servanthood
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Malik ibn Dinar and the broken pitcher
stops.campa: Malik ibn Dinar visits the sick Rabia and finds her whole estate: a broken pitcher she drinks and makes her ablutions from, an old reed mat, and a brick she sometimes uses as a pillow. Grieved, he offers to bring her something from his own rich friends. She rebukes him for the offer as a grievous error: is not her Provider the same as theirs? Has the Provider of the poor ever forgotten them for their poverty, or remembered the rich only for their riches? Since God already knows her estate exactly, she asks, what business has she reminding Him of it through Malik's friends.
stops.quote: Malek, you have committed a grievous error. Is not my Provider and theirs one and the same?... Since He knows my estate, how should I remind Him? Such is His will, and I too wish as He wills.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The broken pitcher, reed mat, and brick pillow, the complete inventory of her sickroom
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Hasan, Malik, and Shaqiq on the lash of the Lord
stops.campa: Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, and Shaqiq of Balkh come together to the sick Rabia and each offers a definition of true faith under suffering. Hasan says none is truthful who does not bear the Lord's lash with fortitude; Rabia calls it egoism. Shaqiq says none is truthful who is not grateful for the lash; she says they need better still. Malik says none is truthful who does not delight in the lash; still not enough, she answers. Pressed to better them herself, she pronounces that none is truthful who does not forget the lash entirely in contemplation of the One who deals it.
stops.quote: He is not truthful in his claim who does not forget the lash in contemplation of his Master.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The four-part exchange on the lash of the Lord, a set-piece of Sufi teaching literature
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, the scholar who reviled the world
stops.campa: A leading scholar of Basra sits beside Rabia's pillow on her sickbed and spends his visit disparaging the world at length, its vanity, its snares, its worthlessness. Rabia tells him plainly that he loves the world very dearly, for it is always the purchaser who disparages the wares he means to bargain down, and a man truly finished with the world would not trouble to mention it at all, for good or ill. As the proverb runs, she says, whoever loves a thing speaks of it often; his lengthy contempt for the world is itself the clearest proof of how much he still wants it.
stops.quote: You love the world very dearly. If you did not love the world, you would not make mention of it so much. It is always the purchaser who disparages the wares.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The scholar's disparagement, answered by the proverb of the purchaser and the wares
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the death of Rabia
stops.campa: When the hour comes for Rabia to die, those attending her, 'Abda among them, are asked to leave the room, and the door is closed behind them. Some time passes with no sound from within. Then a voice is heard from inside, saying: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, well pleased! When those outside open the door at last, they find that she has given up the ghost, alone with the voice that called her, exactly as she has spent every year since the lantern over her head asking to be alone with nothing else.
stops.quote: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, well-pleased!
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry (echoing Qur'an 89:27-28)
suggested_refs: The closed door of the death-chamber, opened only after the voice had already spoken and gone silent
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: Basra, the dream after death, Munkar and Nakir
stops.campa: After her burial Rabia is seen in a dream and asked how she fared with Munkar and Nakir, the two angels who question the dead in the grave. She answers that the youths came and asked who her Lord was, and she told them to go back and say to God: among so many thousand thousand creatures, Thou didst not forget one feeble old woman; I, who have had only Thee in the whole world, will never forget Thee for sending someone to ask me who my God is. The interrogation of the grave becomes, in her telling, one more proof of how closely she is kept.
stops.quote: Those youths came to me and said, 'Who is thy Lord?' I answered, 'Return and say to God, with so many thousand thousand creatures Thou didst not forget one feeble old woman. I, who have only Thee in the whole world, I shall never forget Thee, that Thou shouldst send one to ask me. Who is thy God?'
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry
suggested_refs: The dream of Munkar and Nakir, sealing her story with a final act of devoted defiance
sources: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (tr. Arberry)

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the tomb that Basra and Jerusalem both claim
stops.campa: Basra keeps a tomb for Rabia near the hermitage of her long life, and the pilgrimage guides of Basra point it out across the centuries. But another tradition, gathering strength through the medieval chroniclers of Jerusalem's holy places, points instead to a small domed chamber below a mosque on the Mount of Olives, hung in green, where Muslims venerate her, Christians know the same cave as the grave of Pelagia of Antioch, and Jews as the grave of the prophetess Huldah. One woman's name multiplies across three faiths at a single door in the ground, as if the torch and the water she carried had never gone out.
suggested_refs: The maqam of Rabia al-'Adawiyya at the Chapel of the Ascension complex, Mount of Olives, Jerusalem — a shared pin with margarita_pelagia.journey.json
sources: Museum With No Frontiers, 'Maqam of Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya'
Madain Project, 'Chapel of the Ascension Complex'
